chapter: Tatum, Wiggins and Los Angeles friends
title: Wiggins's trio at the Turban Room and why Tatum and Wiggins were his favorites
summary: He repeats the Turban Room story, dates it to 1952-53, and compares freedom with Wiggins to accompanying Tatum.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Art Tatum: the legend, the piano and the man

blocks.x: So did you and Gerry Wiggins work together other than... I mean, he was in Les Hite's band and you had the intermission trio. But did you two work together any time apart from that?

Oh, yes, indeed. I don't know whether I told this before or not. But after I had come back from Honolulu, I worked with Gerry Wiggins and Bill Douglass. It was Gerry Wiggins' trio. We worked in the Turban Room on Central Avenue, which was sandwiched in between the Alabam and the Dunbar. We worked there I guess off and on for a couple of years.
Yeah. He'd let me off to do record dates and stuff like that.

Anyhow, Tatum used to come in, and this is where Tatum got the idea for the same kind of trio, because he stole us from Gerry, and Bill and I went to work for Tatum. That's how that happened. I didn't mention that before, but that's how that happened. So we worked with Tatum off and on up until the time of his death.
But you started working with Gerry at the Turban Room in what year?
I would say probably 1952, '53, in there.

Oh, probably a couple of years off and on, we worked together. And I have to say that the two joys of my life would Tatum and Gerry Wilson...I mean, Gerry Wiggins. You know, I worked with a lot of piano players who I loved dearly, but the two that I seemed to get along with best would be Gerry Wiggins, number one, because I'm freer with him... With Tatum, it wasn't a case of being free, it was a case of being a good accompanist for whatever he did. Does that make sense?
